question: Prediction of progression from MCI to dementia/AD among ADNI MCI patients from baseline cognitive scores plus structural-MRI measures. P-156 also uses CSF and other modalities. P-211 also uses APOE4 and demographics. The shared channels are clinical/cognitive data and MRI. The endpoints differ: P-156 predicts the latest recorded diagnosis (dementia) with no fixed horizon, and P-211 predicts AD within a fixed window, 5 years for the recorded figure. The rule allows differences in horizon, label definition, cohort, validation and model.
metric: AUC with AUC (ROC area in both papers).

figures.P-156: Ensemble Integration (stacking with random forest), baseline data, evaluated on a random held-out 20% test set: 841 - 672 = 169 patients. The test class split is not printed; the cohort's 34% progressors give about 58/111. AUC 0.81. Hanley-McNeil with 58/111: Q1 = 0.81/1.19 = 0.681, Q2 = 2(0.6561)/1.81 = 0.725, SE = sqrt([0.1539 + 57(0.0246) + 110(0.0689)]/6438) = 0.0377 -> 0.736-0.884. Splits from 50/119 to 66/103 give 0.732-0.888.
figures.P-211: EBM with pairwise interactions, Comb (a), 5-year window, n = 225 (85 AD/140 MCI), 90/10 split, SMOTE, 5-fold CV: AUC 0.92 (abstract; Figure 2 plots the mean with SD bars, and the SDs are not printed). Hanley-McNeil on the 90% training set (76/126): Q1 = 0.92/1.08 = 0.852, Q2 = 2(0.8464)/1.92 = 0.882, SE = sqrt([0.0736 + 75(0.0055) + 125(0.0353)]/9576) = 0.0226 -> 0.876-0.964 (0.878-0.962 on all 225). If 0.92 were an estimate on the 10% test set (about 9/14), the SE would be 0.068 and the interval 0.788-1.000, which contains 0.81. The CV reading is used because the paper says the EBMs 'were tested with the 5-fold cross validation' and plots fold means with SDs. P-211's other figures: about 0.9 at 1 year and lowest at 3 years (the CV value is not printed). The 3-year held-out test AUC is 0.81 with interactions and 0.78 without.
figures.comparison: 0.92 lies above P-156's upper bound (0.884, or 0.888 at the least favourable split), and 0.81 lies below P-211's lower bound (0.876). Each estimate lies outside the other's interval.

matched_figure_check: Neither paper reports a figure under the other's condition. P-156 has no fixed horizon and no AD-only endpoint, and P-211 has no latest-diagnosis endpoint. P-211's 3-year held-out test AUC (0.81) equals P-156's 0.81, but it is not P-156's condition: P-156's endpoint is the last recorded diagnosis at whatever follow-up each patient had, not a 3-year window. That test figure is also the only held-out result P-211 prints, so setting it against P-211's 5-year CV value confounds horizon with validation design. P-211 attributes its 3-year low to patients who had not yet converted (half of its 3-year false positives converted by 5 years). Neither paper isolates horizon, endpoint or validation as the cause of the cross-paper gap.
performance_validity: Passes: 0.92 and 0.81 are below 0.97. Both are internal validations. P-211's figure is a cross-validated mean after SMOTE, and the paper does not say whether SMOTE was applied inside the folds. If it was not, the CV estimate is optimistic. This is recorded as a candidate explanation, not an exclusion.

candidate_explanations.difference: Endpoint and horizon: latest recorded diagnosis of dementia with no fixed horizon, against AD within 5 years with other outcomes excluded. P-211 shows its AUC varies with horizon.
candidate_explanations.quote: The mean AUC using Comb (a) displayed a characteristic pattern of first at about 0.9, then decreasing, reaching a low point at 3 years, followed by a gradual increase until 5 years of follow-up, to about 0.92.
The most recent diagnosis given to each patient (Final DX) was the outcome predicted (stable MCI or progressed to dementia).

candidate_explanations.difference: Validation design: a single held-out 20% test set, against a 5-fold cross-validated mean after SMOTE. P-211's only printed held-out figure (3 years) is 0.81.
candidate_explanations.quote: The dataset is divided into training and test sets with a percentage, respectively, of 90% and 10%. In order to handle the issues of data imbalance, the synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE) is used.

candidate_explanations.difference: Sample: the 5-year analysis uses only the 225 patients with 5-year data (140 MCI/85 dementia), against 841 patients in P-156.
Feature set: P-211 uses cognitive scores, regional FreeSurfer measures, APOE4 and demographics. P-156 uses nine modalities, including CSF, after dropping PET and DTI for missingness.
candidate_explanations.quote: Our feature set includes baseline demographic data such as age, gender, years of education, as well as clinical such as APOE4 status, ADAS13, MMSE, CDRSB, and MRI-related measures, which were used as inputs to the EBMs

candidate_explanations.difference: Model: stacking ensemble over modality-specific models, against an explainable boosting machine with pairwise interactions. On P-211's 3-year test, interactions raise AUC from 0.78 to 0.81.
candidate_explanations.quote: The main performance indicators, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and AUC, were 0.75, 0.78, 0.73, and 0.81 (with interaction effects) compared to 0.72, 0.76, 0.68, and 0.78 (without interaction effects), respectively.

reason: Both papers predict MCI-to-dementia/AD progression in ADNI MCI from baseline cognitive and MRI data and report ROC AUC. P-211's 5-year cross-validated 0.92 (derived interval 0.876-0.964) and P-156's held-out 0.81 (0.736-0.884) exclude each other, and neither figure is near ceiling. No figure in either paper is reported under the other's endpoint. P-211's 3-year test AUC equals P-156's, but it differs from P-156's condition in horizon and matches it only in validation design, so it does not reconcile the pair. The pair qualifies. The candidate explanations (endpoint and horizon, CV with SMOTE against a held-out test, the 225-patient 5-year subset, feature sets, model) are not shown to be sufficient. The verdict assumes the 0.92 is a CV estimate, as the paper states. A 10%-test estimate would not exclude 0.81.

quotes.quote: on a held out test set, the EI-based model performed better (AUC = 0.81, F-measure = 0.68) than the more commonly used XGBoost (AUC = 0.68, F-measure = 0.57)

A randomly sampled 80 % subset of this cohort was used to train all the predictive models for the target problem. These models were then evaluated on the test set, which consisted of the remaining 20 % of the cohort.
The diagnosis of 288 of these patients changed to dementia at a later time point, while 553’s diagnosis stayed as MCI.
The most recent diagnosis given to each patient (Final DX) was the outcome predicted (stable MCI or progressed to dementia).
The five-years prediction accuracy reached 85% (AUC = 0.92) using both cognitive scores and MRI markers.

The dataset is divided into training and test sets with a percentage, respectively, of 90% and 10%. In order to handle the issues of data imbalance, the synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE) is used.
All EBMs were tested with the 5-fold cross validation.

The mean AUC using Comb (a) displayed a characteristic pattern of first at about 0.9, then decreasing, reaching a low point at 3 years, followed by a gradual increase until 5 years of follow-up, to about 0.92.
The results showed that 50% of false-positive MCI patients would convert to AD at the 5-year follow-up
The main performance indicators, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and AUC, were 0.75, 0.78, 0.73, and 0.81 (with interaction effects)
